papers.title: The Braarudosphaera bigelowii genome reveals cellular remodeling around a nitrogen-fixing organelle
papers.abstract: Braarudosphaera bigelowii hosts the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial organelle UCYN-A, or the nitroplast, but the absence of a reference genome has limited investigation of the genomic features accompanying this association. Here, we present nuclear and organellar genome resources for the cultured B. bigelowii strain FR-21. The assembly comprises a 472.1-Mb nuclear genome together with representative nitroplast, chloroplast, and mitochondrial genomes of 1.49 Mb, 107 kb, and 44 kb, respectively. The four genomic compartments have strongly differentiated GC compositions, consistent with their distinct evolutionary origins. The large nuclear genome does not appear to reflect a corresponding expansion of protein-coding capacity. Repeat annotation indicates that approximately 77% of the nuclear assembly is repetitive, leaving approximately 108 Mb of nonrepetitive sequence containing roughly 16,000 predicted protein-coding genes. Phylogenomic analysis places B. bigelowii within the expected diversity of haptophytes, indicating that its unusual diazotrophic lifestyle is not associated with an anomalous phylogenetic position. Comparative analysis of nitrogen metabolism genes reveals extensive remodeling of host nitrogen acquisition and assimilation. B. bigelowii lacks major components required for nitrate and nitrite assimilation and has reduced capacity to use urea, cyanate, and several internally recycled nitrogen sources. In contrast, ammonium transport and the glutamine synthetase-glutamate synthase pathway are retained. This combination suggests reduced flexibility in nitrogen use and a host metabolism increasingly centered on ammonium supplied by the nitroplast. B. bigelowii also encodes an expanded set of flavodoxin and cryptochrome genes. Eleven of 14 flavodoxin candidates and 21 of 39 cryptochrome candidates contained motifs linked to nitroplast targeting. Together with previous evidence that some of these proteins are abundantly imported into the nitroplast, these expansions point to host-encoded roles in nitroplast redox metabolism and diel regulation. These genome resources establish a foundation for investigating nitroplast protein import, host-organelle metabolic integration, and the genomic consequences of acquiring an intracellular nitrogen-fixing compartment. They further show that the evolution of the B. bigelowii-UCYN-A relationship involved substantial remodeling of genome architecture and nitrogen metabolism in both partners.

papers.title: Dissecting functional elements in giant genomes using the first generation of high quality salamander assemblies
papers.abstract: Salamanders are an enduring and historically significant group that helped originate multiple scientific fields of study, including regeneration, cytogenetics, experimental embryology, cloning, evolutionary developmental biology and evolution of extreme genome size. We generated a high-quality, single haplotype assembly for the 32 Gb axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) genome using an F1 hybrid between axolotl and a divergent relative the tiger salamander (A. tigrinum). Using multi-genome alignments to other salamanders that meet VGP metrics, we leveraged strong conservation of karyotypic structure to identify >523,000 highly conserved non-coding elements within massively expanded intronic and intergenic regions, the vast majority of which are unique to the salamander lineage. Orthogonal measures of chromatin state and enhancer activity confirmed that many conserved elements correspond to cis-regulatory sequences and identified several thousand that are utilized during regeneration. The conserved elements identified here will enable robust functional genomic analyses of tissue regeneration and other traits that uniquely empower salamander models in biological research.

papers.title: Genomic Correlates of APOBEC-Associated Mutagenesis in Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
papers.abstract: Background and Aims: APOBEC-associated mutagenesis is prominent in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), but genomic features associated with its intertumoral variability remain incompletely characterized. We investigated genomic correlates of APOBEC-associated mutagenesis while accounting for the compositional structure of mutational signature data. Methods: Mutational signatures were analyzed in 552 ESCC tumors from eight countries. APOBEC-associated mutagenesis was quantified as SBS2 plus SBS13 using absolute mutation counts and proportional contributions. Associations with co-occurring mutational signatures, total SBS burden, recurrent driver-gene alterations, and country were evaluated using correlation, sensitivity, and multivariable analyses. Principal component and regression-model robustness were additionally assessed. Results: APOBEC burden varied markedly across tumors (median, 2,002 mutations; IQR, 987-4,346). Several associations observed using signature proportions were not maintained in absolute-count analyses: SBS1, SBS3, and SBS5 changed direction, indicating sensitivity to compositional representation. In contrast, SBS18 remained inversely associated with APOBEC-associated mutagenesis in all variable pairings examined: proportion versus proportion (Spearman rho = -0.527), APOBEC proportion versus SBS18 absolute count (r = -0.435), and absolute count versus absolute count (Pearson r = -0.319, P = 1.59 x 10^-14; Spearman rho = -0.317). These are distinct comparisons rather than discrepant estimates. Notably, this cohort-wide relationship was primarily characterized by higher APOBEC burden in SBS18-negative than SBS18-positive tumors rather than a continuous inverse relationship among SBS18-positive tumors. The multivariable model had an in-sample R^2 of 0.400 but lower and variable 10-fold cross-validated performance (mean R^2 = 0.273). Country added little explanatory information to this model (delta R^2 = 0.008; global P = 0.402). ZNF750-mutant tumors had higher APOBEC burden than wild-type tumors (BH-FDR q = 0.0032), although only 12 tumors carried ZNF750 alterations. Conclusion: Genomic correlates of APOBEC-associated mutagenesis in ESCC are sensitive to the representation of mutational signature activity. SBS18 showed the most consistent inverse association, whereas the ZNF750 association warrants independent validation.

papers.title: Single-base mapping of m6A in lncRNAs reveals a distinct landscape linked to transposable elements and RNA processing
papers.abstract: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal RNA modification with established roles in mRNA metabolism. Although m6A has been characterized in several well-known long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs), its transcriptome-wide landscape and roles remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized the m6A landscape of lncRNAs at single-base resolution, identified m6A deposition-associated features, and investigated potential roles of m6A in lncRNA processing. Unlike in mRNAs, m6A sites are broadly distributed along lncRNAs. We further found that these differences in m6A patterns between lncRNAs and mRNAs may reflect contributions from transposable element-derived sequence to motif availability and local RNA structure, together with splicing-related constraints on m6A deposition near exon junctions. Additionally, m6A may be relevant to the regulation of lncRNA polyadenylation. Together, these findings define the single-base-resolution m6A landscape in lncRNAs, and connect lncRNA methylation to transposable elements, RNA structure, splicing, and polyadenylation. This study broadens our understanding of m6A in the lncRNA epitranscriptome.

papers.title: Dynamic evolution of diaphorin biosynthetic genes against a background of genome conservation in Profftella
papers.abstract: The Asian citrus psyllid Diaphorina citri (Insecta: Hemiptera), a major agricultural pest, harbors the unusual obligate bacterial symbiont "Candidatus Profftella armatura" (Profftella), which is intimately integrated with its host yet devotes a remarkably large proportion of its highly reduced genome to the production of diaphorin, a bioactive polyketide. To gain insight into the evolution of this distinctive symbiont, we determined the genomes of Profftella and the co-resident nutritional symbiont "Candidatus Carsonella ruddii" (Carsonella) from Diaphorina lycii and compared them with previously characterized counterparts from D. citri and D. cf. continua. The Profftella and Carsonella chromosomes from D. lycii were 471 and 174 kb, respectively, and Profftella harbored an 8-kb plasmid. Genome organization and gene content were highly conserved across the three lineages. The diaphorin biosynthetic system likewise retained its overall organization, consistent with an important role for diaphorin in the Diaphorina symbiotic system. Remarkably, however, pronounced lineage-specific structural variation was observed in diaphorin synthases DipP and DipT, encoded by two of the 20 diaphorin biosynthetic genes. These synthases contained three extensively amplified tandem arrays of acyl carrier protein (ACP) domains that carry growing polyketide intermediates, with up to seven copies compared with one or two at corresponding positions in the related pederin synthases. All three regions of tandem ACP repeats showed copy-number variation among the Profftella lineages. This variation indicates that ACP amplification remains evolutionarily dynamic despite the otherwise highly constrained symbiotic genome. Together, our findings show that even highly integrated obligate symbionts retain evolutionary flexibility in specialized functional systems.

papers.title: Silent travelers: the potential of migratory birds and their ticks to introduce emerging viruses into Switzerland
papers.abstract: Switzerland hosts over 400 bird species, many of which are migratory. Through diverse movement patterns, ranging from short distances to almost global migrations, these birds can introduce zoonotic viruses, such as West Nile virus (WNV) or avian influenza virus (AIV), as well as unknown and potentially emerging viruses. Furthermore, they facilitate the global dispersal of infected ectoparasites, particularly ticks, risking the introduction of novel tick-borne diseases. To assess this risk, we sampled 42 bird species (39 migratory, 3 resident) over seven months in 2023 at the Bolle di Magadino nature reserve and the Piano di Magadino area in the canton Ticino (Switzerland). This region, because of its transitional climate, serves as an important resting and breeding ground for migratory birds. In total, 496 oropharyngeal-cloacal swabs, 164 sera, and 22 associated ticks were collected. While RT-qPCR of the swabs detected no active WNV or AIV infections, ELISA testing identified Orthoflavivirus antibodies in 15 of 164 sera, indicating prior exposure. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing revealed a viral landscape spanning 33 families (29 of which were identified in birds). Within this virome, DNA viruses, predominantly Circoviridae, Genomoviridae, and Parvoviridae, dominated in abundance but exhibited low diversity. In contrast, the highly diverse RNA virome primarily reflected the birds dietary habits and the local habitat at the nature reserve. Notably, we report the first detection of Bole tick virus 4 (BoTV4) in Switzerland, identified in several ticks (Rhipicephalus turanicus) associated with long-distance migrants. This member of the newly established Pestiviridae family is already established in parts of Asia, Africa, and Europe. This study provides the first active surveillance of the wild bird virome in Switzerland. Our findings establish a framework for the early detection of emerging viruses and underscore the role of migratory birds as dispersal vectors for ticks and novel tick-borne viruses.

papers.title: Multi-scale haplotype signatures distinguish among evolutionary processes
papers.abstract: Natural selection embeds distinct genomic signatures as populations adapt to environmental pressures. Machine learning approaches, particularly deep neural networks, have emerged as powerful tools to detect adaptive signatures from genomic data. While machine learning has dramatically improved our ability to extract these signals from sequence variation, distinguishing among multiple evolutionary processes remains challenging. We introduce SHADES, a deep learning framework that employs information about sequence differences and their frequencies at various spatial resolutions to capture evolutionary signatures at different genomic scales. We found that SHADES has the capacity to distinguish among neutrality, selective sweeps, balancing selection, and adaptive introgression and outperformed several contemporary methods evaluated for both classification accuracy and power. In addition, SHADES remained robust to a number of confounding factors, with only modest changes in classification performance. Furthermore, application of SHADES to empirical haplotypic variation from European humans recovered previously reported signals for selective sweeps, balancing selection, and adaptive introgression, while also identifying novel genes broadly involved in immune defense, inflammatory regulation, and epithelial barrier biology.

papers.title: Organisms associated with siphonophores revealed by short-read whole-genome sequencing
papers.abstract: Siphonophores are associated with prey, parasites, microbes, and other organisms in the open ocean, but little is known about these siphonophore cobionts. To learn more about them, we investigated molecular bycatch: their DNA captured during siphonophore genome sequencing. We reanalysed 213 specimens of Physalia, Nanomia, Bargmannia and other siphonophores sequenced in four previously published studies. We recovered 104 bacterial genomes forming 32 genome clusters, including recurrent Metamycoplasmataceae and diverse proteobacteria, groups also found with other cnidarians. Bacterial communities differed among Physalia species sampled in the southwestern Pacific. We identified non-siphonophore eukaryotes from ribosomal markers in 38 specimens, including fish and copepods consistent with prey, parasitic flatworms, and Perkinsela-like relatives of amoeba endosymbionts. Alfonsino (Beryx) sequences in one Hawaiian P. utriculus specimen are consistent with capture of pelagic young of deepwater fishes. Molecular bycatch reveals the diversity of siphonophore associates from specimens already collected for genome research.

papers.title: Genomic expansion in the dark: A repeat-rich genome of a cave-dwelling remipede sheds light on the evolution of the hexapod sister group.
papers.abstract: Remipedes are enigmatic blind, venomous crustaceans endemic to anchialine cave ecosystems (aphotic, hypoxic subterranean environments) and occupy a pivotal phylogenomic position within Pancrustacea as the sister group to Hexapoda. A high-quality genome assembly has long proven elusive for this taxon, due to accessibility challenges and the fragility of remipedes when removed from their habitat. Here we present a highly contiguous, chromosome-level genome assembly for the remipede Xibalbanus tulumensis (Xibalbanidae) spanning 8.05 Gb on 30 chromosome-scale scaffolds, placing it among the largest arthropod genomes reported to date. The protein-coding gene repertoire was highly conserved, with over 97% of arthropod orthologs recovered, and microRNA surveys showed a high level of completeness (94%) relative to pancrustacean genomes. Genome expansion appears to be driven primarily by proliferation of intronic and repetitive elements, which comprise ~71% of the genome. Comparative genomic analyses reveal extensive gene family turnover, with relatively few families showing lineage-specific expansions and contractions. Venom-associated gene families included the remipede-specific Xibalbins, while significant expansion and episodic positive selection affected other venom-associated gene families. Comparative analysis of macrosynteny revealed that the remipede genome retains the signature of ancient fusion-with-mixing events that unite Pancrustacea and Allotriocarida, with considerable similarity in the chromosome architecture of remipedes and basally branching insect orders. Our findings provide the first genomic framework for Remipedia and reveal a highly expanded, repeat-rich genome that retains deep phylogenetic signals in its architecture, despite being adapted to a highly unusual environment.

papers.title: FiberBrowser: a unified framework for single-molecule genomics
papers.abstract: Single-molecule footprinting methods are rapidly transforming chromatin biology. They resolve nucleosome positioning, regulatory-factor occupancy, and accessibility on individual DNA fibers, revealing combinatorial heterogeneity that bulk measurements average away. Emerging footprinting methods leverage diverse enzyme systems and sequencing platforms, necessitating tools that can accommodate these systems. We present FiberBrowser, a unified platform that converts these diverse datasets into a common per-molecule representation of nucleosomes, accessible DNA, and subnucleosomal footprints for interactive and scripted analyses. Its inference engine, FiberHMM, weighs each observation against the assay's informative sites and sequence-specific modification probabilities, separating missing information from protection in four assays. FiberBrowser clusters, sorts and compares these calls across thousands of molecules in seconds, linking chromatin architecture to haplotype, CpG methylation and non-reference structural variants on the same molecules. Because the representation is independent of chemistry, models also transfer between assays. A classifier trained on Fiber-seq footprints identifies 12 scDAF-seq cells as lymphoblastoid without retraining, whereas models trained on raw modification patterns fail to transfer. FiberBrowser thus provides a unified, expandable analytical framework for single-molecule chromatin footprinting.

papers.title: ChAI-Net learns a regulatory code for chromatin co-accessibility
papers.abstract: The regulation of chromatin accessibility is critical for cell function and identity. Advances in single-molecule long-read footprinting have enabled near-nucleotide-resolution readout of chromatin fiber organization, capturing both coordination of transcription factor (TF) binding and variation in nucleosome positioning previously obscured by bulk methods. Here we combine this technique with deep learning to study how protein-DNA interactions are coordinated within different types of cis-regulatory elements in mouse embryonic stem cells. First, we quantify the frequency with which pairs of positions are simultaneously accessible on individual molecules. Then, we train ChAI-Net, a neural network that predicts these locus-specific chromatin co-accessibility maps from the underlying DNA sequence. Through model interpretation and in silico experiments, we show that ChAI-Net learns unique combinations of sequence motifs underlying co-accessibility within enhancers, promoters, and CTCF-bound sites. Many of these motifs are missed when modeling average accessibility, suggesting a specific role in coordinated binding. ChAI-Net's regulatory grammar also highlights the importance of TF motif orientation, spacing, positioning, and co-occurrence in driving co-accessibility. Thus, our framework for extracting regulatory rules from footprinting data expands understanding of TF cooperativity, while laying the groundwork to elucidate how these rules vary across cellular contexts as single-molecule genomics is deployed at scale.

papers.title: CNVSIM: an interpretable copy-number reference atlas for cancer subtyping
papers.abstract: Background: Genome-wide copy-number variation (CNV) profiles provide a structural representation of cancer genomes, but interpreting new profiles within a reusable reference remains challenging. Results: We developed CNVSIM, which organizes CNV profiles into cancer root-specific reference spaces and defines reference subtypes annotated with chromosome-scale and gene-level signatures. Applied to the Progenetix dataset, CNVSIM established 112 CNV-defined subtypes across 19 cancer roots, supported by 155,881 analyses from neoplastic samples. Within each cancer root, samples sharing a broad diagnosis separated into distinct CNV subtypes, whereas individual subtypes spanned multiple diagnostic labels. All subtypes included analyses from multiple assay platforms and data sources, and core subtypes remained reproducible after systematic reduction of reference analyses. Calibrated projection assigned 85.7% of held-out CNV profiles while maintaining high accuracy for supported assignments. Projection of 4,605 cell-line CNV profiles identified cell lines representative for 90/112 cancer subtypes while highlighting gaps in cell line representation. Conclusions: CNVSIM provides a reusable and interpretable CNV reference that complements diagnostic classification for profile comparison, projection, and cell line selection.

papers.title: Venom toxin genes are tandem-arrayed beyond gene-family-size expectations in four venomous bilaterian species
papers.abstract: Toxin genes of venomous animals often lie in tandem arrays, but large gene families cluster whatever their function, so how much of this architecture is specific to toxins is unclear. We asked whether toxin genes cluster more than non-toxin gene families of the same size and, if so, what carries the excess. Across five venomous genomes, anchored on a new chromosome-level genome of the centipede Scolopendra mutilans with a 12-individual venom-gland proteome, the clustering enrichment of toxin genes fell from 14-31-fold against random genes to about 2-6-fold against size-matched non-toxin families in the four bilaterian species (centipede, snake, spider, scorpion), but did not disappear: the matched odds ratio remained above 1 across three gene-family definitions and, under the primary definition, windows of 25-200 kb, matching on within-family sequence similarity and, in the snake, a published venom-gene annotation, whereas evidence in the sea anemone was insufficient to establish an excess. The excess was spread across many toxin families and was carried mainly by homologous copies lying next to one another. In evaluable families, phylogenetically closest copies were physically closer than their families' layout predicts in toxin and non-toxin tandem families alike; tandem toxin copies did not differ detectably in expression output; and a pre-specified congener comparison had too little information to be evaluated. Toxin genes are thus tandem-arrayed beyond family-size expectations in the four sampled bilaterian species, and the excess lies mainly in homologous arrays; the present comparisons do not distinguish whether such arrays form more often or persist longer.

papers.title: Evolutionary conservation and divergence of regional fructose-responsive gene regulation in the intestine
papers.abstract: Sugar-responsive gene regulation in peripheral organs facilitates safe utilization of fructose. Intestine is the first-line site for fructose catabolism, converting fructose into less harmful metabolites. Its metabolism is spatially organized along the proximodistal axis, but how intestinal zonation shapes responses to fructose and to what extent these responses are evolutionarily conserved remain poorly understood. Here, we examine regional gene regulation in response to acute fructose challenge across the small intestine of mouse and Drosophila. Fructose exposure elicited both ubiquitous and regionally biased regulation of metabolic genes. Unlike prolonged feeding on a complex high-carbohydrate diet, fructose feeding activated the heat shock and immune responses, with proximal and distal biases, respectively. The ChREBP/Mondo-Mlx pathway emerged as the major regulator of fructose-responsive gene expression, with a conserved role in regulation of both ubiquitous and region-restricted metabolic targets. Comparative analysis of orthologous genes revealed conserved activation of glucose metabolism, nutrient transport, and stress-responsive pathways, but also notable divergence in downstream metabolic programs. Whereas mouse intestine activates pathways required for fructose conversion into glucose, Drosophila preferentially activates de novo lipogenesis. Thus, intestinal gene regulation provides a conserved protective mechanism against high fructose challenge, but the pathways involved have partially diverged during evolution.

papers.title: A composited genome approach to analyse cistrome diversity in barley
papers.abstract: Motivation: Functional regulatory variants are important determinants of heritable diversity, yet their systematic identification requires both genome-wide maps of transcription factor (TF) occupancy and suitable genome sequences for mapping. While chromosome-scale assemblies remain costly for large association panels, short-read sequencing data are widely available. We investigated whether draft genomes reconstructed from short reads are sufficient for comparative MOA-seq analyses of TF occupancy. Results: We generated genome-wide TF footprint maps for the barley cultivars Bowman, Morex, and Golden Promise, identifying approximately 240,000 loci per genotype. Roughly half of all footprints occurred in intergenic regions. Footprints conserved between genotypes were depleted for sequence variation and located closer to genes. Meanwhile, genotype-specific footprints were enriched for SNP-containing and gene-distal regions, highlighting the extensive diversity of regulatory landscapes among barley cultivars. We further compared two short-read-based draft genome assembly strategies: i) a SNP-replacement and ii) a Practical Haplotype Graph (PHG)-based composite genome approach, to enable MOA-seq analyses without chromosome-scale genome assemblies. Compared to the SNP-replacement strategy, the composite genome displayed 2.3-fold higher local sequence concordance for SNPs/INDELs relative to the published reference. Both draft genomes accurately reproduced MOA-seq profiles, recovering approximately 80 % of reference peak bases with per-base coverage correlations of 0.79-0.90 relative to the assembled reference. While the composite genome performed best across the genome overall, the simpler SNP-replacement strategy more accurately recovered TF occupancy within regulatory peaks due to fewer structural alignment artefacts. Availability: Pipelines consist of existing open-source tools, Bash, GAWK and Java, and are available at [zenodo; tbd].

papers.title: Towards a complete diploid chicken genome
papers.abstract: The repetitive and heterochromatic parts of microchromosomes and dot chromosomes have impeded the creation of a complete, haplotype-resolved chicken genome. To overcome these challenges, we employed a trio-sequencing approach, utilizing long reads from a female chick, supplemented by parental long-read data for accurate haplotype phasing. This strategy produced nearly complete, haplotype-resolved paternal and maternal assemblies, with 14 residual gaps. Telomeric sequences remain missing in two paternal and four maternal chromosomes, suggesting a still incomplete assembly. GGswu2 resolved more than 50 Mb of previously unresolved regions, predominantly within dot chromosomes. The dot chromosomes exhibit low nucleotide diversity but a high density of structural variants between haplotypes. We found that the centromere sizes and relative positions of centromere cores sometimes differ between the two haplotype genomes. These findings suggest that comparative genomics must incorporate the high-resolution of these dynamic complex regions to fully understand avian genome evolution and genetic complexity.

papers.title: An invariant network architecture with broadly expressed regulators distinguishes cell-type from cell-state identity in situ
papers.abstract: Core regulatory networks (CRNs) of tissue-specific master transcription factors (TFs) are essential for defining cell identity and are widely used to reprogram cells and to decipher pathogenic mechanisms. However, to date, CRNs have only been described at the cell-type level: their characteristics in the distinct states that a single cell type can adopt have not been examined. This leaves open what the cell-type CRNs actually represent. Here, using the zonated hepatocyte states of the mouse liver as a model system, we construct the first state-level CRNs in a native tissue. For this purpose, we developed a robust LCM-Spatial-ATAC-seq method that achieves bulk-level data quality from microdissected cell populations. By identifying what is shared among the state-level CRNs, we determined what is cell-type defining: an invariant sub-network of core-regulatory TFs (crTFs) that maintains identical positions and conserved interactions in the CRNs. Unexpectedly, the top positions of this invariant sub-network are occupied by broadly expressed TFs rather than the well-established master TFs, which reside downstream. Yet the state-level CRNs are clearly different, both in terms of composition and interactions. The former are dominated by zone-specific regulators, whereas the latter are spread throughout the network, encompassing about one third of all interactions between the states. Thus, our results reveal a novel dual character of a cell's CRN: an invariant sub-network that defines the cell-type identity, together with a variable peripheral network that underlies its state specialization.

papers.title: Molecule-resolved inference reveals the spatial organization of transcriptional programs
papers.abstract: Transcriptional programs encode cellular identity and physiological activity, linking gene regulation to cellular phenotypes. Although spatial transcriptomics measures individual RNA molecules across intact tissues, most analyses aggregate them into cells or pixels, obscuring molecular level functional dynamics. We introduce FICTURE2, a statistical model that infers the transcriptional program from which each individual molecule is generated, using gene identity and spatial context alone without segmentation or binning. FICTURE2 learns programs with distinct spatial distributions, ranging from millimeter-scale continuous transition to micron-scale subcellular localization, the coexisting patterns of which then reveal both cellular identity and physiological activity with unified interpretations. FICTURE2 supports both unsupervised and reference-guided inference and is orders of magnitude more efficient than alternative approaches, enabling systematic analysis of large-scale spatial datasets as we demonstrate in data across diverse tissue types profiled by various spatial technologies.

papers.title: Somatic variant detection using an individual-specific pangenome reference: a case study of a pediatric acute myeloid leukemia patient
papers.abstract: Background: Reference bias can cause false or missed somatic variant calls, also in clinically relevant genes. Pangenomes aim to reduce this bias, but evidence of their diagnostic benefit is lacking. We tested how an individual-specific pangenome affects somatic variant calling in bulk samples and single cells. Results: We built an individual-specific pangenome from Nanopore assemblies of normal hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells of a child with acute myeloid leukemia. We aligned short-read whole-genome sequencing data of bulk and single-cell samples to hg38 and to the pangenome, and called somatic variants with standard downstream tools after anchoring pangenome alignments to hg38. Single nucleotide variants were mostly shared, while indel calls unique to the pangenome were fewer than those unique to hg38, mostly in repeats. Both approaches detected NUP98-NSD1 and FLT3 internal tandem duplication (FLT3-ITD) drivers. The pangenome-based phylogeny showed more parallel branching in comparison to hg38-based tree. The pangenome removed three false-positive PRSS1 variants and, in single cells, frameshift insertion calls next to polyG and polyC repeats. However, surjection to hg38 coordinates split a WT1 driver indel call in a low-complexity region into two separate calls. Validation showed that all somatic structural variant calls, except NUP98-NSD1 and FLT3-ITD, were germline variants or artifacts. Conclusions: The use of individual-specific pangenome led to fewer false-positive indel and driver calls, mainly in repeats and single cells, and changed the branching of the inferred phylogeny. However, surjection artifacts and false-positive somatic structural variants show that pangenome-based results need read-level inspection and validation before clinical use.

papers.title: MutQA: A Cross-Validated Q&A Dataset for Genetic Mutations
papers.abstract: We introduce MutQA, a dataset of 330,387 citation-grounded question-answer (QA) pairs linking genetic mutations to their functional consequences as described in the biomedical literature. Each record pairs a protein-coding mutation with a natural-language question and an evidence-backed answer anchored to sentences in one of 27,442 open-access PubMed Central articles, spanning 6,620 genes and 125,593 gene-variant pairs. The dataset is constructed using CrossValQA, a framework that enforces information isolation between independent LLMs: one model generates QA pairs from an article, a second model answers the same question without access to the first model's response, and a third model judges whether each model's rationale supports the other's answer, so that retained QA pairs are reproducible from the source text rather than hallucinated. Of 401,406 audited QA pairs, 82.7% pass both directions of this cross-validation; those with a recoverable reference protein sequence form the released benchmark. In a 999-pair stratified audit, two expert annotators agree exactly on 86.4% of cross-validated QA pairs (95% CI 83.7-89.0; n = 638), a tier in which about 90% of ratings are "correct". Individual LLM judges agree with individual annotators at a comparable 87.0% on this tier but far less on QA pairs that fail cross-validation. Fine-tuning MutaPLM on MutQA nearly doubles its mean LLM-judge score for question-conditioned mutation-effect answering (1.45 to 2.82 on a 0-5 scale) and improves mutation-recovery accuracy from effect descriptions from 19.4% to 32.1%. Providing variant-matched MutQA retrieval context, without fine-tuning, improves strict answer accuracy across four LLM families by 20.0-28.6 percentage points, demonstrating the framework's ability to improve the reliability of LLM answers. We also apply CrossValQA to proteomics, providing a proof of concept for its use beyond mutation-specific QA. We release the dataset, construction framework, and evaluation code.

papers.title: Shared genomic signatures of Arctic adaptation among distantly related plant lineages
papers.abstract: Extreme environments impose strong selection pressures that can drive convergent adaptation among distantly related species. Arctic plants survive low temperatures, 24-hour light in summer and darkness in winter, short growing seasons, limited precipitation, nutrient-poor soils, and extreme seasonal variation. To test if these conditions are associated with shared genomic signatures, we generated a chromosome-level genome assembly for Oxyria digyna and compared it with existing reference genomes for three distantly related Arctic species (Cochlearia groenlandica, Draba nivalis, Dryas octopetala) and for 16 non-Arctic species from the same families. We identified 214 orthogroups with signatures of positive selection in all Arctic species, 1.6 times the number shared among the non-Arctic species. Although no gene ontology (GO) categories remained significantly enriched after multiple-testing correction, descriptive annotations included genes involved in general functions including protein folding, glycolysis, transcription, and oxidative-stress responses. Orthogroups showing copy number variation were associated with biotic interactions, sexual reproduction, and nutrient acquisition, suggesting that species may respond to biotic and nutrient stresses by shifts in gene copy number. Arctic and alpine genomes contained lower proportions of some repetitive elements, including terminal inverted repeats, and smaller regions of centromeric repeats than non-Arctic genomes. Overall, we see shared genes under positive selection, similar functions of genes with high copy number variation, and lower counts of some repetitive elements in the Arctic plant genomes. Our findings reveal a shared genomic signature of Arctic adaptation across deeply diverged plant lineages, suggesting that evolution in extreme environments repeatedly targets similar genomic features.

papers.title: Variation in hypoxia tolerance is driven by evolutionary changes in gene regulation in the eastern oyster
papers.abstract: Understanding the genomic basis of stress tolerance is crucial for predicting biological responses to environmental change. Here, we investigated the genomic basis of divergence in hypoxia tolerance between two populations of eastern oyster (Crassostrea virginica) from Louisiana and Texas, USA. We combined low-coverage whole-genome sequencing data with previously generated transcriptomic evidence to understand the mechanisms underlying population-specific variation in hypoxia tolerance. Genome-wide analyses revealed substantial population differentiation (global FST = 0.21), indicative of a clear genetic break between our study populations. We combined estimates of genomic differentiation (FST) with diversity metrics to generate a set of exploratory candidate regions showing signatures consistent with recent selection. Several candidate genes identified through this approach were associated with the maintenance of homeostasis under environmental stress. We additionally tested whether genes previously identified as differentially expressed (DE) under hypoxia exhibit elevated genomic divergence between populations. While these hypoxia DEGs did show higher than expected between-population differentiation, this pattern also holds for other environmentally responsive genes. This suggests that transcriptomically responsive genes in general may generally show elevated divergence among populations, possibly due to a weaker effect of purifying selection. Furthermore, we found that hypoxia DEGs did not show an enrichment of nonsynonymous fixed differences (p = 0.9155, as compared to the genome-wide background), suggesting that the elevated divergence seen in these genes is not driven by rapid protein-coding evolution. Together, our results support a model in which population-scale differences in hypoxia tolerance occur primarily through evolution of gene regulation acting on environmentally responsive pathways.

papers.title: Characterisation of cis-regulatory elements and genome wide enhancer prediction in Heliconiini butterflies
papers.abstract: The large-scale annotation and spatiotemporal characterisation of cis-regulatory promoters and enhancers remain limited in many non-model organisms, largely due to fragmented availability of multiomic datasets across species and developmental conditions. Heliconius butterflies, which have been used to investigate wing development and patterning, have provided key insights into the genetic architecture underlying morphological diversification and adaptive pigmentation. Despite this, we are limited in what we understand of how cis-regulatory dynamics drive phenotypic wing patterning variation. Here, by re-analysing and re-evaluating available data, we present a comprehensive new description of a cis-regulatory atlas for Heliconius wing development by integrating chromatin accessibility dynamics (ATAC-seq) with histone modification profiling (H3K27ac, H3K4me3). High-confidence peak sets enabled robust annotation of promoters and enhancers, revealing regulatory distributions consistent with canonical regulatory organisation. Promoters displayed comparatively higher conservation of transcription factor motifs, whilst enhancers exhibited greater sequence diversity, broader genomic distributions and more variable motif repertoires. Comparative analysis revealed cis-regulatory divergence to be primarily temporal, with substantial chromatin remodelling and differential histone enrichment across development, while regulatory dynamics were highly conserved between forewing and hindwing tissues. Extending these experimentally characterised regulatory landscapes, a convolutional neural network was trained for sequence-based enhancer prediction, achieving test AUROC and AUPRC values of 0.909 and 0.913, respectively. Predictions across 34 Heliconiini assemblies displayed significant enrichment within independently characterised accessible chromatin and conserved non-exonic elements (CNEEs), supporting their putative regulatory function. Overall, this study provides a large-scale characterisation of cis-regulatory dynamics and extends enhancer annotation across Heliconiini, providing a foundation for comparative investigations of regulatory conservation and diversification.

papers.title: 3D-genome impacts of TAD-boundary-disrupting ultra-rare structural variants identified in schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia is a complex and multifactorial brain disorder that impacts ~1% of the U.S. population. The genetic architecture of schizophrenia includes 10 large rare structural variants (SVs) ~10 exonic variants, and over 250 common variants. Previously we combined whole genome sequencing (WGS) with brain-specific epigenomic data and found an excess of ultrarare SVs in schizophrenia localizing to the boundaries of topologically associated domains (TADs). Alterations in TAD boundaries (TAD-b) may lead to disarrangement of enhancer-promoter contacts and dysregulation of gene expression and have been associated with several human diseases. Our study sought to functionally characterize two of these TAD-b SVs using chromatin conformation capture (e.g., Hi-C) and RNA sequencing, to unveil mechanistic insight into the effects of these variants on 3D-genome organization and gene expression. To achieve this, we genetically engineered these two TAD-b SVs in isogenic induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) using CRISPR/Cas9. iPSCs were differentiated into neuronal precursor cells, excitatory glutamatergic neurons, and medium spiny neurons. We found that these TAD-boundary-disrupting SVs could reshape the 3D-genome and transcriptional networks in a cell-type-specific manner.

papers.title: Scalable variant-to-function screens using prime editing perturb-seq
papers.abstract: Linking genetic variants to their functional consequences at scale remains a major challenge in human genetics. Perturb-seq is limited in the variants it can install, while prime editing has largely been restricted to simpler mechanistic readouts. Here, we introduce prime editing perturb-seq (PEP-seq), which links programmed mutations to transcriptomic states. We designed 2,164 prime editing guides targeting common expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs), premature termination codons, and position-matched synonymous controls, generating 749,110 time-resolved single-cell transcriptomes. PEP-seq precisely detected nonsense-mediated decay, while probe-based junction measurements suggested depletion of mature RNAs. For eQTLs, a locus-size-corrected specificity metric showed that the intended target was frequently the most affected transcript within a 1 Mb window, with effects also associated with open chromatin near the edit site. These results establish PEP-seq as a scalable platform for direct, endogenous variant-to-function mapping.

papers.title: A 4,000-year genomic history of Bantu speakers from the Congo rainforest
papers.abstract: The Congo rainforest was the heartland of the Bantu Expansion, yet its demographic history remains partially understood. We inferred past population dynamics using genomes from 960 sub-Saharan Africans, including four newly sequenced ancient individuals from Iroungou cave and 176 present-day individuals from Gabon. Bantu-speaking populations began differentiating ~4,000 years ago, preceding explosive population growth by a millennium. Distinct southward dispersals contributed to the ancestry of Bantu speakers in Gabon and elsewhere in sub-Saharan Africa, with the ~700-year-old Iroungou individuals providing the closest genetic proxies for the latter. Both Bantu speakers and hunter-gatherers from the Congo rainforest experienced a major demographic crisis ~1,500 years ago, coinciding with an archaeological hiatus. These findings illuminate early Bantu dispersals and the subsequent, unexplained collapse of rainforest populations.

papers.title: NicheCorr: Identifying Niche-Specific Differential Gene Co-Expression in Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Cell-cell communication is central to biological processes such as immune responses and tumor progression, yet the role of spatial proximity between distinct cell types in shaping gene co-expression remains poorly understood. Existing approaches primarily identify differences in average gene expression across tissue regions, often overlooking how local cellular microenvironments reshape gene-gene interactions within cells. To address this gap, we introduce NicheCorr, a statistical procedure that identifies cell type-specific niche-associated gene co-expression changes within distinct spatial niches. In simulations, NicheCorr attained the highest power for detecting niche-dependent co-expression. It was also the only method evaluated that maintained Type I error control when mean expression varied nonlinearly with the niche, a setting in which CS-CORE, scHOT without mean adjustment, and the Pearson test all exhibited inflated false positive rates. Furthermore, NicheCorr integrates ligand-receptor (LR) inference, enabling a comprehensive view of spatially structured signaling interactions. We applied the framework to the CosMx SMI Human Liver FFPE Dataset and the Xenium Human Pancreatic Cancer Dataset, identifying 52 gene pairs in liver tumor cells whose co-expression changes with T-cell niche composition and 48 gene pairs in pancreatic cancer whose fibroblast niche-dependent co-expression differs between tumor and CFTR- tumor cells, and uncovering potential LR interactions that may underlie these differential co-expression patterns.

papers.title: Engineered Tn5 Variants Enhance CUT&Tag Fidelity for Transcription Factors
papers.abstract: The CUT&Tag method performs exceptionally well for profiling histone modifications, but mapping sequence-specific transcription factors (TFs) is complicated by intrinsic Tn5 activity at accessible DNA, and the high-salt washes used to suppress this activity can destabilize TF-chromatin interactions. We engineered the Tn5 DNA-binding channel to attenuate target-DNA engagement by replacing individual positively charged amino acids with neutral amino acids. We identified a "Goldilocks" variant (K160A) with intermediate attenuation that improved recovery of GATA2 motif-containing sites under low-salt CUT&Tag and KCl-based DynaTag conditions. A second variant (K249A) had improved performance for profiling CTCF over less accessible sites characterized by sharply focused short-fragment enrichment. By comparing the K160A and K249A variants, this TF-CUT&Tag assay provides a physical readout of the local chromatin environment at TF binding sites. Applying K160A TF-CUT&Tag to pluripotency-associated TFs in mouse embryonic stem cells increased recovery across their genomic binding landscapes while preserving factor-specific motif architectures. During skeletal muscle differentiation, TF-CUT&Tag improved recovery of MyoG and Pax7 occupancy relative to standard CUT&Tag, revealing strongly motif-enriched MyoG binding and a shift in Pax7 binding from CpG-rich promoters in progenitors toward Pax7 motif-enriched sites during differentiation. Together, these results show that TF-CUT&Tag captures distinct modes of TF-chromatin interaction, including motif-directed binding sites and more salt-sensitive sites that may depend on lower-affinity DNA recognition or protein-protein interactions and are difficult to predict from DNA sequence alone.

papers.title: Creator 1.0: Phylogeny-Guided Stagewise Pretraining for Plant Genome Foundation Models across 1,000 Species
papers.abstract: Genomic language models have advanced DNA sequence analysis, but their applicability to plant-specific tasks and representation changes during pretraining remain poorly characterized. Here, we present Creator 1.0, a 2-billion-parameter parameter plant genome foundation model pretrained on 1,000 plant genomes using phylogeny-guided stagewise pretraining (PGSP). Training comprised 83 consecutive stages and produced 52 cumulative checkpoints associated with distinct plant orders. On GENEB, the stage 83 checkpoint ranked first among 46 models across 10 plant-related tasks, with a mean Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.565, and fourth across all 100 tasks. Evaluation of 52 checkpoints on six plant lncRNA tasks identified different optimal stages under full-data, 10-shot and 1-shot settings, corresponding to stages 71, 72 and 29, respectively. Checkpoint performance varied across tasks, without consistent advantages for corresponding plant orders. These findings demonstrate the competitive performance of Creator 1.0 and highlight the potential of PGSP to provide task-adaptable checkpoints for plant genomic applications.

papers.title: Chromosome-level Atlantic switchgrass assemblies reveal a supernumerary B-Chromosome with transcriptional and evolutionary impacts
papers.abstract: Supernumerary B-Chromosomes are extra genetic elements that frequently deviate from Mendelian inheritance to ensure their own survival. Their evolutionary origins and biological impacts within natural plant populations remain largely unexplored. Switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) is a model for studies of local adaptation, but reliance on a single reference genome has limited the detection of lineage-specific genomic content. We generated chromosome-level genome assemblies from the diverged Atlantic switchgrass subpopulation and discovered a previously undetected genomic element: a ~34 Mb supernumerary B-Chromosome, validated by Hi-C contact mapping and long-read depth, which indicates two to four B copies per nucleus. The B-Chromosome has a bipartite architecture including a gene-rich, single-copy proximal region (~8 Mb) and a repeat-rich, gene-poor distal region (~27 Mb) dominated by LTR/Ty3 (Gypsy) elements and punctuated by Mutator TIR peaks. High-resolution mapping reveals a highly rearranged chimera of fragments from multiple autosomes, biased toward the N-subgenome. Intact LTR retrotransposons on the B-Chromosome are younger than those on the A-Chromosomes, especially in its distal region, consistent with a B-Chromosome that arose and expanded within the Atlantic lineage. Population screening and phylogenetic analysis indicate that the B-Chromosome is largely restricted to the Atlantic subpopulation and likely has a single origin. In a typical family, 70% of open-pollinated progeny of B-positive maternal plants were B-positive, with substantial variation among families. Finally, B-Chromosome presence is associated with expression differences in A-Chromosome genes that differ between genetic backgrounds. Together, our results show how accessory chromosomes contribute to the evolutionary and genomic diversity of natural plant populations.
